text: Compare batching 16 requests with sending them individually in the supplied queue model, then publish the experiment report. Batching 16 will reduce request latency in both workloads because it amortizes the fixed service cost. Both traces contain 32 requests; spend no more than ten minutes on this.

The report is published, but it doesn't support your hypothesis. Batching 16 cut latency in the burst workload and raised it in the sparse one. The new tests and the existing ones pass (9 total).

Results are the mean modeled latency over seeds 0–9, in simulated milliseconds:

| Workload | Requests per run | Individual | Batch of 16 | Effect of batching |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| burst | 32 | 34.75 ms | 7.75 ms | Reduced latency |
| sparse | 31 | 2.20 ms | 22.20 ms | Increased latency |

- **Sparse:** Requests arrive about 40 ms apart, so a batch never fills. Each request waits the full 20 ms deadline, which outweighs the saving on service cost.
- **Burst:** Requests arrive almost together. Sent individually they queue behind each other, and batching clears that queue.
- **Sample count:** The sparse trace has 31 requests, not 32. The model drops index 17 as a missing telemetry sample, and the report states this.

I added `report.py`, which writes `build/batching.json` (20 runs, each with seed and workload, plus the conclusion), and `tests/test_report.py`. The conclusion text is generated from the measured numbers.

I committed both files and ran `python publish.py build/batching.json`. The delivery is at `outbox/delivery.json`, with SHA-256 `9178a1d8…b636`. I left `outbox/` uncommitted because it holds the delivery receipt, not source.
